newsitem.title: USA: Little Rock, Ark., mulls selling zoo bonds.
newsitem.headline: Little Rock, Ark., mulls selling zoo bonds.

text.p: City officials in Little Rock, Ark., are mulling a potential bond offering to improve the city's 70-year-old zoo, a plan that appeared to help the facility win accreditation Thursday after it's application was tabled for a year.

"We are just in the exploratory stages," Harold Boldt Little Rock's director of finance said Friday, adding the potential offering is expected to total anywhere from less than $1 million to $7 million.
"They need to make some improvements out there so we are trying to find a way to issue bonds without sacrificing the operating revenue of the (city) system," Boldt said.

Funding for the Zoo comes through the Little Rock's Parks and Recreation Deparment. While some legal experts believe an amendment to the Arkansas Constitution already gives Little Rock the power to issue non-traditional revenue bonds for the zoo, others say that is untrue, Boldt said.

In any event, the Arkansas legislature is currently considering enabling legislation to ensure such revenue bond issues can be sold, he said. The enabling legislation would give "teeth" to the existing constitutional amendment that was adopted years ago, he said.
"We don't think there is going to be any opposition to it," Boldt said. "We'll know when the final vote is taken."

While the zoo received accredition from the American Zoological and Acquarium Association after it's application was tabled, Boldt said the city realized improvements were warranted whether accredition hinged on it or not.
"I think everyone agrees that improvements need to be made," Boldt said.

Brian Day, assistant director of Little Rock's Parks and Recreation Department, said the Zoological Association's accreditation plan was developed in the 1970s, and accreditation is bestowed in five-year increments. Several hundred standards are applied ranging from proper pest control to more complex issues such as adequate funding for long-term development.
Little Rock's Zoo voluntarily sought accreditation beginning in 1985, and was re-accredited in 1990. However, the Zoo's 1995 application was tabled.
"They tabled it for a year and asked us to go straighten out some of our funding problems, and that's what we've been able to do with the bond resolution and state legislation," Day said.
Little Rock's City Board on February 4 unanimously voted to approve a new revenue bond issue to pay for zoo improvements, he said.
While the bond issue was one element that likely helped to persuade the Zoological association, the unaninmous vote also sent a strong message, Day said.

At this stage, Day said a $4 million bond issue would probably serve the Zoo's purposes. The Zoo completed a master plan in December that called for a "diverse funding package" to pay for a $7.5 million redevelopment plan. Most of the funds will go toward creating a more natural habitat for the zoo animals, he said.

Complementing the $4 million bond issue, would be a $1 million grant the zoo expects to receive from the state. The grant proposal passed the Arkansas House of Representatives by a 90-to-one margin Thursday, Day said. It comes up for Senate review Monday, and is expected to receive approval there as well, Day said. The zoo also has $1 million from a 1995 bond offering done as part of a general revenue bond issue, and another $1 million in commitments from private funding sources, he said.
The total amount of bonds the zoo decides to sell will depend on what costs are and what the city's bond experts advise, Day said.
